summary: Haiti lies in the western part of the island of Hispaniola in the Caribbean; it was founded by a slave revolution in 1804 and is the world's first republic established by former slaves.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1697 France acquired the western part of Hispaniola from Spain and established the colony of Saint-Domingue; the Code Noir promulgated in 1685 required slaves to be baptized as Catholics, so Catholicism became the official faith. After Haiti's independence in 1804, the Vatican long refused to recognize the new regime, and it was not until a concordat was signed in 1860 that French clergy again led the church. Catholicism was the state religion until the 1987 constitution and is still the largest religion today.

ranking.name: Protestant Christianity
ranking.description: In 1824 Haitian president Boyer invited free Black American immigrants, who brought Methodism and the Baptist church. During the American military occupation of 1915–1934, American missions entered in large numbers; in the late 20th century Pentecostal and Baptist churches expanded rapidly in the countryside and cities, and international relief after the 2010 earthquake further increased the influence of Evangelicals, so the proportion of Protestants is now close to thirty percent.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious are mostly young people in cities such as Port-au-Prince. Long-term political turmoil, natural disasters and poverty, along with disillusionment with religious institutions, have led some people to no longer identify with a particular religion, but the proportion is still relatively low.

ranking.name: Vodou
ranking.description: Vodou originates with the slaves from West and Central Africa (Fon, Yoruba, Kongo and others) who were trafficked to Saint-Domingue, who combined their ancestral spirit beliefs with Catholic saints. The Bois Caïman Vodou ceremony of 1791 is regarded as the starting point of the Haitian Revolution. The Catholic Church launched "anti-superstition" campaigns persecuting Vodou followers in 1896, 1913 and 1941–1942, and the government formally recognized it as a religion only in 2003. Very few people identify as following only Vodou, but a Haitian saying goes "seventy percent Catholic, thirty percent Protestant, one hundred percent Vodou", showing how widespread it is.

religion.background: Haiti's religious history is inseparable from slavery and revolution. The French colonists made Catholicism the official religion and forced slaves to be baptized, while the slaves preserved African beliefs under the cover of Catholicism, forming Vodou. The slave revolution from 1791 was rallied through Vodou ceremonies, and in 1804 the world's first republic founded by freed Black slaves was established. After independence Catholicism remained the state religion and cooperated with the state in suppressing Vodou; in the 20th century American influence brought rapid growth of Protestantism. Today the three faiths are interwoven, forming the unique face of Haitian religion.

language.official: Haitian Creole and French are the official languages.

ranking.name: Haitian Creole
ranking.description: Haitian Creole formed on the plantations of French Saint-Domingue in the 17th–18th centuries, with most of its vocabulary from French and its grammar influenced by West African languages such as Fon, as a product of communication between trafficked Africans and the French. Although almost the entire population has it as their mother tongue after independence, it was long regarded as an "informal" language; the education reform of 1979 first introduced it into schools, the 1987 constitution made it an official language alongside French, and the Haitian Creole Academy was established in 2014.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French is the language of the colonial metropole, and after independence in 1804 it remained the language of government, law, education and the elite, and was the sole official language until 1987. But only a small, well-educated minority can use it fluently, so French has long been a dividing line between social classes, and many people face the difficulty of learning in school in an unfamiliar French.

language.history: The language of the indigenous Taíno of Hispaniola disappeared with colonization, leaving only place names such as "Haiti" (Ayiti, meaning mountainous land). In the 17th century French colonists and hundreds of thousands of West African slaves formed Creole on the plantations. After independence in 1804 French remained the official and elite language, while Creole was the everyday language of all, forming a typical stratified bilingual society. From the late 20th century language movements promoted the standardization of Creole writing and its use in education, and the 1987 constitution formally recognized its official status.

ranking.name: Soup joumou (pumpkin soup)
ranking.description: A thick soup with a pumpkin base stewed with beef, potato, carrot, cabbage and macaroni, with the aroma of spices and chili.
ranking.history: In the French colonial period, pumpkin soup was regarded as a dish of the slave owners, and the enslaved could only cook it but were not allowed to eat it. After Haiti declared independence on January 1, 1804, the people celebrated freedom by drinking pumpkin soup, and ever since, every year on Independence Day (New Year's Day) households across the country cook pumpkin soup and share it with neighbors. In 2021 Haitian soup joumou was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, symbolizing freedom and dignity.

ranking.name: Griot (fried pork)
ranking.description: Cubes of pork shoulder are marinated in sour orange juice, garlic, herbs and chili, first stewed and then fried until crisp outside and tender inside, often served with pikliz and fried plantain.
ranking.history: The pig is a livestock animal that the Spanish brought to the Caribbean in the 16th century and was long an important asset in Haitian villages. The sour orange marinade combines the citrus introduced in the colonial period with the spicy taste preferred by Africans. In the 1980s, because of the African swine fever epidemic, an international aid program culled Haiti's native Creole pigs, dealing a heavy blow to farmers. Griot is the most popular dish at weddings, birthdays and holiday parties, and is regarded by many as one of Haiti's national dishes.

ranking.name: Pikliz
ranking.description: A spicy pickle made of shredded cabbage, carrot, onion and Scotch bonnet peppers soaked in white vinegar, tangy and refreshing, cutting the greasiness of fried foods.
ranking.history: The name comes from the French-influenced "pickles", reflecting the linguistic influence of French colonization, while the heavy use of chili continues the taste tradition of the Caribbean indigenous peoples and Africans. In a tropical climate, vinegar pickling extends the keeping time of vegetables. It is an indispensable side with almost every Haitian fried dish, used to balance the richness, and every household keeps its own jar ready.

ranking.name: Bannann peze (fried plantain)
ranking.description: Green plantains are cut into pieces, fried, flattened, and fried a second time, crisp outside and fluffy inside, and eaten sprinkled with salt; it is an essential item on Haiti's fried food platter.
ranking.history: Plantains were introduced to the Caribbean by the Spanish from Africa and the Canary Islands in the 16th century and became one of the main foods of slaves. The "peze" in the name comes from the French for "pressed" and describes how it is made. It is the most common side dish on Haitian streets and in homes, often eaten with griot, fried chicken and pikliz, forming the familiar Haitian "fritay" platter.

ranking.name: Black mushroom rice (diri ak djon djon)
ranking.description: Rice cooked in the deep black liquid steeped from the local specialty dried black mushrooms; the rice is black with a rich mushroom aroma, often with green peas or shrimp added.
ranking.history: Black mushroom rice is a specialty of northern Haiti, and the "djon djon" used is a small black mushroom that grows in northern Haiti, famous for its strong aroma. It was at first a local dish of the northern region and later became the feast rice for weddings, festivals and important family gatherings across the country. The dish shows the food culture of Haitians creating distinctive dishes from local specialties, and is one of the tastes of home most missed by Haitians abroad.
